title: Scaling Out: Many Servers, One API
summary: Run the API as many stateless instances behind a load balancer, find services with discovery and gateways, and learn what the network costs.
intro: One server is simple, and it's where every API starts. Then exam week arrives, every student books a room at 8 a.m. on Monday, and the one machine runs out of room, or crashes, and Roombook is down for everyone. Running many copies of the API fixes both, and it changes the rules your code has lived by: memory is no longer shared, requests land on whichever copy is free, and the network between machines can fail in ways a function call never does. This lesson covers why and how APIs scale, what breaks when you run two copies of FastAPI Roombook, where state has to go instead, how load balancers, gateways, and service discovery send each request to the right place, and what a network of machines costs you. The next lessons build on it: Redis, then reliability, then databases at scale.

steps.title: From one server to many
steps.body:
Up to now, Roombook has been one program on one computer. Every request goes to that one process, which keeps whatever it likes in memory and talks to one database. That's the right way to start, and many real APIs never need more. It's worth knowing exactly where it stops working.

## What one server can't do

- **Handle unlimited traffic.** A machine has so many CPU cores, so much memory, and so many network connections. When Monday's rush needs more than that, requests queue up, slow down, and start timing out.
- **Survive its own failure.** A **single point of failure** is a part whose failure takes down the whole system. With one server, that's the server, and also the disk, the power supply, and the operating system update that needed a reboot.
- **Deploy without downtime.** Starting a new version means stopping the old one, and for those seconds, every request fails.

**Scaling** means growing a system to handle more work. There are two ways, and the difference shapes everything that follows.

## Vertical and horizontal

**Vertical scaling**, or scaling up, means a bigger machine: more cores, more memory, faster disks. Your code doesn't change at all, which makes it the easiest first step. But machines only get so big, the price climbs faster than the size, and a bigger single machine is still a single point of failure.

**Horizontal scaling**, or scaling out, means more machines, each running a copy of the API. Each running copy is called an **instance**. Ten small instances can handle ten times the traffic of one, you can add an eleventh during exam week and remove it after, and when one instance dies the other nine keep answering. A deploy can replace them one at a time, which is called a **rolling deploy**, so the API never goes down.

```diagram scaling-out-vertical-horizontal
Scaling up makes one machine bigger. Scaling out adds more machines like it.
```

The catch is that horizontal scaling needs your code to work when it's one of many copies. That's what most of this lesson is about.

## The shape of a scaled-out API

Many instances need a few things around them:

```diagram scaling-out-architecture
Clients talk to one address. The load balancer spreads requests over the instances, which share one database and one Redis.
```

- Clients still use one address, `api.roombook.example`. Behind it sits a **load balancer**, a server that receives every request and passes each one to one of the instances. The opening lessons met it briefly, and a later part covers it in full.
- The instances are identical copies of the same build, with the same configuration.
- They share the things that hold state: PostgreSQL for the data, and **Redis**, an in-memory data store that the next lesson introduces, for what's shared and short-lived, like caches and rate-limit counters.

## A monolith first

Roombook is a **monolith**: one program, one codebase, deployed as one unit, with bookings, rooms, auth, and feedback inside it. The other style is **microservices**: many small programs, each owning one area, each with its own database and its own deploys, talking to each other over the network.

Scaling out doesn't need microservices. Ten copies of the monolith behind a load balancer is horizontal scaling, and it's how most APIs grow. Microservices solve a different problem: many teams who need to ship separately. They bring a heavy cost in network calls, distributed failures, and data split across databases, which the last part of this lesson describes. Start with a monolith, keep its modules separate inside, as the layers lesson did, and split a piece out only when there's a clear reason.

steps.title: Stateless servers
steps.body:
Put two instances behind a load balancer and run the same requests as before. Most of them work. A few fail in ways that look random: Ada signs in and her next request says she isn't signed in, a room shows as free after it was booked, a reminder email arrives twice. Each failure has the same cause. The code assumed that the next request would come back to the same process.

## What stateless means

A server is **stateless** when it keeps nothing between requests that another instance would need. Every request carries what it needs, its token or cookie, its body, its parameters, and everything else comes from shared stores. Then any instance can answer any request, the load balancer is free to send each one anywhere, and an instance can die or be replaced without anyone noticing.

HTTP itself is stateless, as the web course said. The trouble is state your app adds on top. These are the usual suspects:

- **Sessions in memory.** Ada signs in on instance A, which remembers her session in a map. Her next request goes to instance B, which has never heard of it, and answers 401.
- **Caches in memory.** Each instance caches room availability separately. A booking on A clears A's cache, and B keeps showing the slot as free until its copy expires.
- **Files on local disk.** An uploaded photo lands on A's disk, and a request for it on B finds nothing.
- **Counters in memory.** A rate limit of 100 requests a minute, counted separately on ten instances, is really 1,000.
- **Scheduled jobs.** A job that sends tomorrow's booking reminders at 6 p.m. runs on every instance, so every student gets ten reminders.
- **Long-lived connections.** A live availability stream, held open on A, never hears about a booking made on B.

```diagram scaling-out-memory-session
Ada signs in on instance A, which keeps her session in its memory. Her next request lands on B, which has no such session.
```

## Where state goes instead

The fix is to move each kind of state somewhere every instance can reach:

| State | Where it goes |
|---|---|
| Data: bookings, rooms, users | PostgreSQL, as it already is |
| Sessions | PostgreSQL, as the authentication lesson stored them, or Redis, where the next lesson moves them |
| Caches, counters, rate limits | Redis, in the next lesson |
| Files | Object storage, like Amazon S3, which stores files by name over HTTP |
| Jobs | A queue, and a scheduler that runs a job once, not once per instance |
| Who the caller is | The request itself: a cookie or a token |

Roombook already did most of this. Bookings have lived in PostgreSQL since the PostgreSQL lesson, sessions moved there in the authentication lesson, and access tokens carry the caller's identity, so any instance can check them. The examples show both sides: sessions kept in memory breaking across two instances, and a booking made on one instance read back from the other.

## Many copies on one machine

Your First FastAPI Project showed why one Uvicorn worker uses about one CPU core: it's one process, with one event loop and one GIL. `fastapi run --workers 4` starts four worker processes that share one port, and the operating system hands each new connection to whichever worker accepts it first.

Every worker has its own memory, its own module-level variables, and its own database pool. So `--workers 4` on one machine is already four instances, and a dict of sessions in one worker is invisible to the other three. The third example shows exactly that. It also means your database sees workers times machines times pool size connections, which the lesson on databases at scale comes back to.

## Disposable instances

The **Twelve-Factor App** is a well-known list of rules for apps that run in the cloud, written by engineers at Heroku in 2011. Its sixth rule says it directly: processes are stateless and share nothing, and anything that must last goes in a backing service, like a database. A related rule says instances are **disposable**: they start fast and stop cleanly at any moment. A platform adding an instance for exam week, or removing one at 3 a.m., should never lose anything.

examples.title: Signed in on one instance, unknown on the other
examples.prompt: `sessions_demo.py`, a small demo that keeps sessions in a dict, started twice with Uvicorn on ports 8001 and 8002. Sign in on 8001, then ask both who you are with the same cookie.
examples.code:
curl -s -c cookies.txt -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' --json '{"email": "ada@roombook.example", "password": "correct horse battery staple"}' http://localhost:8001/v1/auth/login
curl -s -b cookies.txt http://localhost:8001/v1/me
curl -s -b cookies.txt http://localhost:8002/v1/me
examples.explanation: The login answered 204 and set a session cookie, which `-c` saved. Instance 8001 knows the session, so `/v1/me` returns Ada. Instance 8002 got the very same cookie, since cookies for `localhost` go to every port, and answered 401, because the session exists only in 8001's memory. Behind a load balancer, that's a user who signs in and is signed out on the next click, or every other click. Roombook's real sessions live in PostgreSQL, from the authentication lesson, so they don't have this problem.

examples.title: State in the database, shared by every instance
examples.prompt: Two copies of the real Roombook, on 8001 and 8002, using the same PostgreSQL. Book on 8001, then read the booking from 8002.
examples.code:
curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} %header{location}\n' -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" --json @booking.json http://localhost:8001/v1/bookings
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" http://localhost:8002/v1/bookings/1001 | jq -c '{id, roomId, startsAt, status}'
examples.explanation: The booking was created on 8001, and 8002 read it back at once, because neither instance kept it: both asked PostgreSQL. The token worked on both too, since each instance checks its signature with the same secret and needs to remember nothing. That's the stateless shape: the instances are interchangeable, and the state lives in a shared store. `-w '%header{location}'` printed the response's `Location` header, and `jq -c` printed a few fields on one line.

examples.title: Four workers, four separate memories
examples.prompt: The same in-memory demo, as one server with four workers on port 8001. Sign in, then ask who you are eight times.
examples.code:
fastapi run sessions_demo.py --port 8001 --workers 4
curl -s -c cookies.txt -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code}\n' -X POST http://localhost:8001/v1/auth/login
for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w '%{http_code} ' -b cookies.txt http://localhost:8001/v1/me; done
examples.explanation: The first command runs in its own terminal. The login landed on one of the four workers, and only that worker's dict holds the session. Each later curl opened a new connection, which the operating system handed to whichever worker took it: the first went to the worker that knew Ada, and the other seven to workers that didn't. Nothing in the code changed between one worker and four, which is exactly why this bug hides until the day someone adds `--workers`.

steps.title: Load balancers and reverse proxies
steps.body:
Clients know one address, and there are many instances behind it. Something has to receive each request and decide which instance gets it, keep sending traffic only to instances that work, and hide the fact that there are many at all. That's the job of a load balancer, and it's the piece every scaled-out API has.

## Reverse proxies and load balancers

A **proxy** is a server that passes messages along on someone else's behalf. A **reverse proxy** sits in front of servers: clients connect to it, it forwards each request to a server behind it, and sends the answer back, so clients never talk to the servers directly. A **load balancer** is a reverse proxy that spreads requests over many instances of the same service. In practice the words overlap, and one program often does both.

Common ones are nginx, HAProxy, Envoy, Caddy, and Traefik, which you run yourself, and the managed ones every cloud sells, like AWS's Application Load Balancer.

## Layer 4 and layer 7

Network people describe a connection in layers. Two of them matter here. **Layer 4** is TCP, connections and bytes, and **layer 7** is the application protocol, here HTTP.

- A **layer 4** load balancer forwards whole TCP connections without reading them. It's fast and works for any protocol, but it can't see a path or a header, and every request on a kept-alive connection goes to the same instance.
- A **layer 7** load balancer reads each HTTP request. It can send `/v1/bookings` to one group of instances and `/docs` to another, add headers, retry a failed request on another instance, and end TLS. Most API traffic goes through one.

## Choosing an instance

- **Round robin** takes the instances in turn. Simple, and fine when requests cost about the same.
- **Least connections** picks the instance with the fewest requests in flight, which helps when some requests are slow.
- **Hashing** picks by a hash of something in the request, like the client's address or a header, so the same key always goes to the same instance.
- **Weights** send more traffic to bigger instances, or a little to a new version, to try it carefully.

## Health checks

A load balancer has to stop sending requests to an instance that's down. It asks each one, every few seconds, for a cheap endpoint like `GET /healthz`, the one Roombook has had since the first project. A few failed answers in a row and the instance leaves the rotation, and a few good ones bring it back. The lesson on timeouts, retries, idempotency, and circuit breakers covers what a health endpoint should check, and how an instance leaves the rotation before it stops.

```diagram scaling-out-load-balancer
The load balancer ends TLS, adds X-Forwarded-For, and sends requests only to instances whose health checks pass.
```

## TLS, and who the client is

HTTPS from the web course needs a certificate, and with many instances it's simplest to keep it in one place: the load balancer. It ends the encrypted connection, which is called **TLS termination**, and forwards plain HTTP to the instances over the private network, or encrypts again if the network isn't trusted.

That leaves the instances blind: every connection now comes from the load balancer's address, over HTTP. So the load balancer adds headers saying what it saw. `X-Forwarded-For` lists the client's address, and each proxy along the way appends the address it received from. `X-Forwarded-Proto` says the original scheme, `https`. The standard `Forwarded` header carries the same facts, and fewer tools use it.

Those headers are only true if the proxy wrote them. A client can send `X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4` itself, so your app must trust the headers only on connections that come from your own proxy. The example shows how in FastAPI. Rate limits and audit logs depend on getting this right.

## Sticky sessions, and why to avoid them

A load balancer can pin each client to one instance, usually with a cookie of its own, which is called **sticky sessions**. It makes in-memory sessions seem to work, and it's a trap. Load stops being even, since one busy client stays on one instance. When that instance dies or is replaced in a deploy, everyone pinned to it loses their state at once. And scaling out stops helping the users who are already pinned. Making the servers stateless fixes the cause, so you don't need the patch.

## CDNs

A **CDN**, a content delivery network, is a reverse proxy spread around the world. It keeps copies of responses on servers near each user and answers from the nearest one. For an API, that suits public `GET`s that change rarely, like the list of buildings, when the response's `Cache-Control` header allows it.

examples.title: Trusting only your own proxy
examples.prompt: Behind a load balancer at 10.0.0.5, start Roombook so Uvicorn trusts forwarded headers from that address only.
examples.explanation: Uvicorn, under `fastapi run`, reads `X-Forwarded-For` and `X-Forwarded-Proto` when `--proxy-headers` is on, which is the default, but only from the addresses in `--forwarded-allow-ips`, which defaults to `127.0.0.1`. Here 10.0.0.5 is the load balancer's address, so `request.client.host` becomes the real client and `request.url.scheme` becomes `https`. Never pass `*` on a server the internet can reach directly: then anyone can send `X-Forwarded-For: 1.2.3.4` and become 1.2.3.4, which breaks rate limits and audit logs.

examples.title: A load balancer in front of three instances
examples.prompt: An nginx configuration that spreads requests over three Roombook instances on one private network, ends TLS, and adds the forwarded headers. nginx's format isn't highlighted, so it's shown as text.
examples.explanation: `upstream` names the group of instances, and `least_conn` picks the one with the fewest requests in flight. `max_fails=3 fail_timeout=10s` is nginx's simple health check: after three failed requests, it stops sending to that instance for ten seconds. The `server` block listens on 443 with the certificate, so TLS ends here, and `proxy_pass` forwards plain HTTP to the group. The headers pass on the original `Host`, the client's address, appended to any `X-Forwarded-For` already there, and the scheme.

steps.title: Finding services: discovery and gateways
steps.body:
As long as Roombook is one service behind one load balancer, finding it is easy: its address is in the configuration. That changes when the system grows into several services, each with several instances that come and go: the booking API, a notification service that sends emails, maybe a search service. Two questions come up. How does one service find the instances of another right now? And what do outside clients talk to, when there's more than one service behind the front door?

## Service discovery

**Service discovery** is how a program finds the current addresses of a service's instances. Instances start and stop all the time, in deploys and as the platform adds or removes them, so a list typed into a config file would always be wrong.

- **DNS**, from the web course, is the simplest discovery system there is. Give the service a name, like `notifications.internal`, and have DNS answer with the current addresses. Keep the TTL short, so old addresses expire fast.
- A **service registry** is a small database of who's running where. Each instance registers when it starts, sends heartbeats while it runs, and drops out when it stops or stops answering. Consul and etcd are common ones.
- **Kubernetes**, a system that runs containers across many machines and restarts them when they fail, has discovery built in. A Kubernetes **Service** gives a group of instances one stable name and address, and routes each connection to an instance that's ready, as the example shows.

Discovery comes in two styles. In **server-side discovery**, the caller sends every request to one address, a load balancer or a Kubernetes Service, which knows the instances. In **client-side discovery**, the caller asks the registry for the list and picks an instance itself, which saves a hop but puts that logic in every client. Either way, health checks feed the list: an instance that fails them stops being handed out.

## API gateways

Outside clients shouldn't need to know how many services you run, or which one answers which path. An **API gateway** is a reverse proxy that is the single front door for all of them. It routes each request by its path or host to the right service, and it's the natural place for jobs every service would otherwise repeat:

- checking the caller's token or API key, once, before any service sees the request
- rate limits per caller
- adding a request id, and logging every request in one format
- ending TLS, and answering CORS preflights

```diagram scaling-out-gateway
One gateway in front of several services. It checks auth and limits, then routes by path.
```

A gateway can also be a **backend for frontend**, the BFF from the opening lessons: a gateway shaped for one client, like the mobile app, that combines several services' answers into the one response that screen needs. Kong, Envoy-based gateways, and the managed gateways cloud providers sell are common choices.

## Gateway, load balancer, or service mesh?

The three overlap, and the words get used loosely. A **load balancer** spreads requests over the instances of one service. A **gateway** sits in front of many services and handles the edge: who's calling, how often, and where each path goes. A **service mesh** handles traffic between your own services: a small proxy, called a sidecar, runs next to every instance and takes care of retries, timeouts, encryption, and metrics for every call, so the services' code doesn't have to. Istio and Linkerd are service meshes. Roombook, as one monolith, needs a load balancer, maybe a gateway one day, and no mesh.

examples.title: A stable name for changing instances
examples.prompt: A Kubernetes Service for Roombook. Kubernetes runs the instances, called pods, from a separate Deployment file, each with the label `app: roombook`.
examples.code:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: roombook
spec:
  selector:
    app: roombook
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 8000
examples.explanation: This gives every pod labeled `app: roombook` one name, `roombook`, and one stable address inside the cluster. Another service in the same namespace just calls `http://roombook/v1/rooms`, and Kubernetes's DNS answers for the name, then spreads the connections over the pods that are ready. Port 80 on the Service goes to port 8000 in each pod, where Roombook listens. When pods are replaced in a deploy, the Service's list updates by itself, which is server-side discovery with nothing to run but Kubernetes.

steps.title: What the network costs you
steps.body:
Inside one process, a function call either returns or throws, and it takes nanoseconds. Between machines, every call crosses a network, and a network adds three things you never had to think about: it's slow, it fails, and sometimes it fails without telling you. Scaling out makes more of your calls cross it. This part is the price list, so the next lessons, which pay it, make sense.

## Three outcomes, not two

When your code calls another machine, the call can succeed, fail with an error, or neither: no answer comes, and you can't tell what happened on the other side. The example shows the third kind. The server accepted the connection and never answered, and curl gave up after two seconds with no way to know whether the server did the work.

That's a **partial failure**: part of the system works and part doesn't, and the caller can't see which. The lost reply is the classic case:

```diagram scaling-out-lost-reply
The booking was saved, and the reply never arrived. The client can't tell this from a failure.
```

In step 1 the mobile app sends a booking, and in step 2 Roombook saves it. In step 3 the reply is lost: a phone moved between cell towers, a load balancer restarted, a timeout fired one millisecond early. The app sees an error. If it gives up, Ada thinks she has no room when she does. If it retries, she may get two bookings. Neither is right, and the fix, an idempotency key that makes the retry safe, is the heart of the lesson on timeouts, retries, idempotency, and circuit breakers.

## The network is not your friend

In the 1990s, engineers at Sun Microsystems wrote down the **fallacies of distributed computing**, beliefs that feel true and cause outages. A few of them:

- **The network is reliable.** It isn't: packets drop, connections reset, and machines restart.
- **Latency is zero.** Every call costs time, a millisecond inside a data center and far more across the world. A request that makes five calls one after another waits for all five.
- **The network is secure.** Traffic between your own services can be read or faked too, which is why meshes encrypt it.
- **The topology doesn't change.** Instances come and go every day, which is why discovery exists.

So every call across the network needs a **timeout**, a limit on how long to wait, since "forever" is the default in more clients than you'd like, as the client in the lesson on curl, Postman, and OpenAPI showed. It needs a decision about retrying, which is only safe for some calls. And it needs a plan for when the other side is down for minutes.

## Copies disagree

Once data lives in more than one place, the copies can disagree. A cache in Redis says Turing is free, and PostgreSQL says it was booked a second ago. A database replica, a read-only copy of the primary database, is a moment behind. Two services, each with its own database, each hold half the truth.

**Strong consistency** means every read sees the latest write, as if there were one copy. **Eventual consistency** means copies agree if you wait a little, and a read might see the past in the meantime. Roombook chooses per piece of data: bookings must be strong, since two people must never hold Turing at once, which is why the overlap check lives in PostgreSQL, while a room's average rating can be a minute out of date and nobody minds. The lesson on databases at scale comes back to this.

Clocks disagree too. Every machine's clock drifts, so never order events from different machines by their timestamps. Let the database decide what happened first.

## Not every call needs an answer now

Some work doesn't have to happen inside the request. When Ada books a room, she needs the 201 now. The confirmation email can go out a few seconds later, and if the email provider is down for ten minutes, her booking shouldn't fail because of it. So instead of calling the email service, the API drops a message into a **queue**, a list of jobs kept by a server called a **message broker**, and answers at once. A separate process, a **worker**, takes each job off the queue and does it, retrying if it fails.

```diagram scaling-out-queue
The API puts a message on a queue and answers at once. Workers take messages off and do the work.
```

Queues smooth out bursts, since workers drain the queue at their own pace, and they keep a slow or broken service from slowing the API. They also scale on their own: more work, more workers. RabbitMQ, Kafka, and Amazon SQS are common brokers, and Redis can act as one, as the next lesson shows. In Python, Celery, Dramatiq, and arq run background jobs on a broker, and arq uses Redis. How to use them safely, when a message can arrive twice, is part of the lesson on timeouts, retries, idempotency, and circuit breakers.

## The bill

None of this means you shouldn't scale out. It means each machine you add buys capacity and availability, and you pay in timeouts to set, retries to make safe, copies to keep in step, and failures to plan for. The next three lessons pay that bill one piece at a time: Redis for shared state, then reliability, then databases at scale.

examples.title: A call that neither succeeds nor fails
examples.prompt: In another terminal, `nc -l 127.0.0.1 8002` listens on port 8002: it accepts connections and never answers. `--max-time 2` makes curl give up after two seconds.
examples.explanation: `nc`, short for netcat, is a tool for raw network connections, standing in here for a server that's stuck. curl connected, sent the request, and waited. After two seconds it gave up with error 28, a timeout, having received nothing at all. From the client's side there's no way to know what happened: the server might be stuck, the request might still be running, or the work might be done and the answer lost. Without `--max-time`, curl would have waited until the operating system gave up, which can take minutes. Every client in production needs a limit like this, and the lesson on curl, Postman, and OpenAPI set one in Python with httpx2.
examples.output:
curl: (28) Operation timed out after 2006 milliseconds with 0 bytes received
exit code: 28

examples.title: A message for the email worker
examples.prompt: What the API puts on the queue after Ada's booking commits: a small JSON event that says what happened, not what to do about it.
examples.explanation: An **event** records a fact, `booking.confirmed`, rather than a command like "send an email", so more workers can react to it later, a calendar sync or a statistics job, without the API changing. The `id` is unique per event, so a worker that receives the same message twice can tell, and skip it. `createdAt`, when it happened, and the booking's fields give the worker everything it needs without calling the API back. Roombook's webhooks, from the lesson on API styles, send events of the same shape to other people's servers.

recap:
- Vertical scaling buys a bigger machine. Horizontal scaling runs many instances, survives the loss of one, and deploys without downtime.
- Scale out a monolith first. Microservices solve team problems, and bring network problems with them.
- Stateless servers keep nothing between requests, so any instance can answer any request.
- Sessions, caches, files, counters, and jobs move to shared stores: PostgreSQL, Redis, object storage, and queues.
- A load balancer spreads requests, health-checks instances, ends TLS, and adds X-Forwarded-For, which you trust only from your own proxy.
- Avoid sticky sessions. Service discovery finds instances, and a gateway is the front door for many services.
- Across a network a call can succeed, fail, or never answer, so every call needs a timeout and a plan for retries.
- Copies of data disagree for a while, so choose strong or eventual consistency per piece of data, and use queues for work that can wait.
